ecommerce_d00.subject: Eight photos of the bag. This view was missing.
ecommerce_d00.preheader: Start with a question your product page still leaves unanswered.
ecommerce_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. These emails share ways to help people understand a product through its images and make an informed choice.

Illustrative story.

Laura runs a handbag shop. She has prepared eight photos of one bag: beside a plant, on a table, in beautiful light.

Then a message arrives:

“What does the back look like?”

She opens the product page. None of the photos shows it.

Laura looks through other questions and finds three different needs:

“What does the back look like?” → a rear view or a way to explore the shape.

“Will my laptop fit?” → reliable internal measurements.

“How does it open?” → a demonstration of the fastening.

You can use the same distinction for your product. The buyer’s question helps you choose what to show.

If they need to explore its shape, that can guide a small 3D test. If they need a measurement, provide it from a reliable source.

Laura’s next image now had a specific job.

Choose one product page and complete: “My buyer needs to see ___ to decide ___.”
ecommerce_d00.action: Choose one product page and complete: “My buyer needs to see ___ to decide ___.”

ecommerce_d02.subject: Laura’s favourite bag had to wait
ecommerce_d02.preheader: Three conditions for choosing a small 3D test.
ecommerce_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Laura was going to try 3D with the most striking bag in her shop. Then she looked at the data.

It received few visits. Another bag prompted questions about the shape of its pockets, and she had good photos to check it against.

She chose the second one.

For a small test, look for three things together: a specific visual question, a product that already gets attention, and enough references to review the result.

Laura’s brief read:

“Product: bag with a side pocket. Question: how far the pocket projects. Check: its profile and fastening position. References: photos of the actual product. Destination: its product page.”

You can adapt this example. If you have not chosen a product, it gives you a starting point. If you already have a model, use it to identify the question you want to evaluate.

You can prepare that test in easyrender. Before any paid step, check the current cost and decide how much you want to spend evaluating this case. One product can teach you something before you commit to a catalogue.

Write a test brief naming the product, question, detail to review and real reference.
ecommerce_d02.action: Write a test brief naming the product, question, detail to review and real reference.

ecommerce_d05.subject: What to check when the product starts turning
ecommerce_d05.preheader: A published case and a question for reviewing your own test.
ecommerce_d05.body:
Published case from Shopify.

Rebecca Minkoff added 3D models to its product pages after receiving questions about its products. Shopify reports that visitors who interacted with the models were 27% more likely to place an order than those who did not. This is an observed comparison; those visitors may have had greater purchase intent to begin with.

Source: https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/rebecca-minkoff

For your test, ask what someone can now understand by turning the product.

If you wanted to show a side pocket, review that pocket: its shape, position and relationship to the rest of the bag. An impressive rotation that changes this detail does not fulfil the brief.

Your note might read: “The profile is visible; the fastening position matches the reference; the back still needs checking.”

If you have an easyrender result, this helps you decide whether it suits the intended use. If not, prepare the same checklist from your references before generating it.

Another brand’s experience suggests a possibility. Your review turns it into a decision about your product.

Write a review note identifying one checked detail and any information still missing.
ecommerce_d05.action: Write a review note identifying one checked detail and any information still missing.

ecommerce_d10.subject: The image was there. The buyer could not find it.
ecommerce_d10.preheader: Try a short mobile check before adding more content.
ecommerce_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Laura showed someone a new product page on her phone.

“Can you see the pocket on the side?”

They swiped through several photos and stopped. The view was there, but far from where they expected to find it.

Laura had worked out what to show. She still needed to check whether people could find it.

You can try a product page or draft with a concrete question. For the bag: “Where is the fastening?”, “What does the side look like?” or “Where are the measurements?”

Ask someone to answer using only the presentation. Watch where they look, what they find and where they need help. This does not need to become a long survey.

If you have a reviewed asset, test it where it will be used, alongside reliable photos and information. Also check that people can keep shopping while a visual resource loads.

If the asset is not ready, you can test the planned gallery order.

Laura moved the side view. Her next check would show whether it was easier to find.

Test one question on a product page or draft and note the first point of difficulty.
ecommerce_d10.action: Test one question on a product page or draft and note the first point of difficulty.

ecommerce_d20.subject: The second product could take more work
ecommerce_d20.preheader: Decide what carries over before expanding your test.
ecommerce_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Laura had prepared one bag and wanted to continue with a similar one. The references revealed a difference: the second bag had a fastening barely visible in the photos.

The earlier process could guide her, but it did not resolve that detail.

Before expanding, she wrote:

“Reuse: the review criteria and destination. Change: the fastening references. Still to estimate: the time needed to check it.”

That note avoids treating every product as the same amount of work.

If you have tested a product, use what you observed across preparation, generation, review and adaptation. The useful cost also includes the work needed to accept the result.

If you have not tested yet, write down what you expect to reuse and leave the rest as unknown. Those are not demonstrated savings.

You can evaluate another case with easyrender once you know what you want to learn and its current cost. Expanding is easier to judge when you can distinguish repeated work from work that is still new.

For a possible second product, note what you can reuse, what changes and what remains to be estimated.
ecommerce_d20.action: For a possible second product, note what you can reuse, what changes and what remains to be estimated.

ecommerce_d28.subject: What decision can your test support?
ecommerce_d28.preheader: Expanding, adjusting and waiting each need a reason.
ecommerce_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Laura brought one finding to the meeting: people were turning the bag in the viewer.

“What should we do with the rest of the catalogue?” someone asked.

The counter showed that the viewer was being used. To decide on the next investment, Laura needed more information.

She separated three questions: does the page answer the original question more clearly, how much work did the asset take, and is there enough evidence to discuss commercial results?

Your closing note might read: “The pocket’s shape is clear; preparation was manageable; we do not yet know whether purchases changed. Next step: keep observing the test.”

To evaluate sales, compare visitors assigned to comparable groups, ideally at random. Looking only at people who used the viewer selects visitors who may already be more interested. For returns, wait until the return window closes.

If you have not tested yet, your note can identify the unanswered question or missing resource. You do not need to invent a result to make a useful decision.

Choose expand, adjust or postpone, and write down the evidence or specific uncertainty behind that choice.
ecommerce_d28.action: Choose expand, adjust or postpone, and write down the evidence or specific uncertainty behind that choice.

furniture_d00.subject: The sofa was going in the middle of the room
furniture_d00.preheader: Its position changes what the buyer needs to see.
furniture_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. This series will help you prepare furniture presentations that give people useful information for their decision.

Illustrative story.

Mateo shows a customer a sofa. Every photo places it against a wall.

“I want it in the middle of the room. Is the back upholstered in the same way?”

For her, the back would be the first thing people saw when entering.

Mateo notes three needs: show that part, confirm the space it occupies, and explain the finish. Each needs a different reference.

You can apply this example to one piece: “It will stand in the centre of the room, visible from all four sides. I need to show the back and provide verified measurements.”

A 3D model can help people explore the shape. Dimensions need a reliable source, while texture and feel need samples or a suitable description.

Before your next presentation, consider where the person using the piece will see it from. That simple question can change which view matters most.

Describe one intended position and the side or detail that matters there.
furniture_d00.action: Describe one intended position and the side or detail that matters there.

furniture_d02.subject: Mateo prepared the test before generating
furniture_d02.preheader: One piece, useful references and a criterion you can check.
furniture_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Mateo opened a folder of chair photos. There was a clear front image and two others taken in the shop.

He almost discarded those two. Then he noticed that one showed the support beneath the seat and the other showed the backrest’s curve.

They would help him review the result, even if they were not the input image.

His brief read: “Represent this chair so we can explore its shape. Check the backrest, legs and seat support against photos of the real product.”

You can prepare a test this way: a familiar piece, a clear input image and references for checking the important details. Separate what you want to show from what you will need to verify.

Even when a workflow uses one image, additional references can help your review. That does not mean the system processes all of them as inputs.

Before a paid operation in easyrender, check the current cost and define the scope of your test. If you already have a model, use the same brief to guide its review.

Prepare the input image, review references and three features to check for one piece.
furniture_d02.action: Prepare the input image, review references and three features to check for one piece.

furniture_d05.subject: The chair had an extra bar
furniture_d05.preheader: What to check before using a model in a presentation.
furniture_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Mateo turned a chair model and noticed a bar beneath the seat.

The image looked convincing. But the product photo had no such bar.

He started comparing it with the specific chair he needed to show.

You can make that review with three questions: are the same parts present, does it preserve the features that identify the design, and what can you not check yet?

A useful note might read: “Backrest: matches the reference. Lower support: needs review. Back: another photograph is needed to check it.”

With an easyrender result, the note helps you decide whether it suits the presentation you are preparing. If you do not have a result yet, write the three checks for your next test.

Measurements need their own reliable sources. A difference that changes the product being sold needs resolving before publication, even when the overall image is attractive.

Mateo could explain why this version was not ready for approval. He had a specific detail to investigate.

Sort your review or review plan into checked, needs correction and missing information.
furniture_d05.action: Sort your review or review plan into checked, needs correction and missing information.

furniture_d10.subject: Three armchairs, three different photo styles
furniture_d10.preheader: Help people compare pieces using the same criteria.
furniture_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Mateo sent three armchair options. One was photographed close up, another in a large room, and the third from above.

“Which takes up less space?” the customer asked.

The images suggested different sizes but could not answer the question.

Mateo prepared the same fields for each piece: intended use, verified dimensions, finish and an equivalent view. He kept the current price in its own field.

You could start with this example: “Armchair A · reading · dimensions from the technical sheet · fabric checked against the sample · front and side views.”

The comparison does not need to pretend that the images are to scale. Written measurements and their source support that decision.

Reviewed models may provide comparable views or shape exploration in a compatible destination. If you do not have them yet, prepare the same structure using the references available.

Mateo’s conversation could now focus on which piece best suited the customer’s intended use.

Prepare two options with matching fields and one specific comparison question.
furniture_d10.action: Prepare two options with matching fields and one specific comparison question.

furniture_d20.subject: The next chair was not quite as simple
furniture_d20.preheader: Decide what to repeat across a collection.
furniture_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Mateo wanted to extend his test to a collection. The first chair had a simple structure. The next added arms and openings in its backrest.

Before repeating the same brief, he compared the differences.

He kept the destination and review method. He changed the detail list: the arms, openings and their positions now needed checking too.

This is a practical way to prepare a collection. Group pieces by features that affect their review, then choose a representative from each group before assuming they require equal work.

Your note might read: “Group: chairs with arms. Shared criterion: commercial presentation. Additional review: joints and openings. Time needed: still to be observed.”

If you have already tested, use what you learned. If not, the note lets you anticipate differences without claiming savings you have not measured.

Repeating a process in easyrender is easier to evaluate when you know what stays the same and what changes for each piece.

Group two or three pieces by review difficulty and choose a representative from one group.
furniture_d20.action: Group two or three pieces by review difficulty and choose a representative from one group.

furniture_d28.subject: Fewer questions arrived. Mateo checked the visits too.
furniture_d28.preheader: Close your test without confusing different signals.
furniture_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Mateo noticed fewer enquiries about a piece and thought the new presentation was working.

Then he checked how many people had seen it. Visits had fallen too.

He needed more than a count of messages.

To evaluate your presentation, bring together three related observations: how many people or proposals had access, which questions arose, and what decisions people could make. Separate questions about shape from questions about measurements, fabric or delivery.

A closing note might read: “The back is easy to find in the usability check; measurements are still missing; there is not enough volume to conclude anything about sales.”

If you tested, fill in the note with your observations and the work involved. If you have not tested, identify the information you need to decide whether preparing it is worthwhile.

You can expand, adjust or postpone the presentation. What matters is knowing why you chose that next step, without turning fewer enquiries into a sale you have not verified.

Choose expand, adjust or postpone and note the evidence or missing information behind your decision.
furniture_d28.action: Choose expand, adjust or postpone and note the evidence or missing information behind your decision.

agency_d00.subject: The client asked for a render. They needed a deliverable.
agency_d00.preheader: One sentence can turn a vague brief into something that can be approved.
agency_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. These emails share ideas for taking a visual asset from the brief to a deliverable your client can use.

Illustrative story.

Inés is preparing a quote. She has written “3D product model”.

Her client asks:

“What does that include for the product page?”

They are discussing the same item, but have not agreed on the deliverable.

She rewrites the proposal: “We will prepare a representation of this product to review its shape. Delivery will include the agreed file, the reference used and the checks carried out in the intended destination.”

You can use that distinction to describe your own work: the product, its use and evidence that it is ready for that use.

If easyrender produces part of the work, this definition helps you review the result and explain what your service includes. Formats, adaptations and conditions must match what you actually deliver.

Inés could now ask the client whether that was the deliverable they needed.

Rewrite one brief in a sentence naming the product, intended use and specific deliverable.
agency_d00.action: Rewrite one brief in a sentence naming the product, intended use and specific deliverable.

agency_d02.subject: Before the catalogue, one piece they could approve
agency_d02.preheader: An example of a pilot with a clear beginning and end.
agency_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Inés’s client wanted an entire catalogue prepared. Some products had details that were hard to see in their photos.

She proposed starting with one representative piece and agreeing how it would be approved.

Her note read: “Product: chair with arms. Use: commercial presentation. Reference: approved photographs. We will review the shape, visible parts and file in the agreed destination. The catalogue owner will approve it.”

The brief is small, but it allows the team to observe preparation, results and review work.

You can adapt it for your own test or a client project. Choose a piece that teaches you something about the catalogue. Picking only the easiest one may leave later work undiscovered.

Before producing it with easyrender, gather references for checking the details and review the current cost of any paid operation. Agreeing to the pilot does not approve work on the whole catalogue.

If you already have a generated piece, the same criteria can identify what needs checking before you present it.

Write a one-piece brief covering use, references, approval criteria and the person responsible.
agency_d02.action: Write a one-piece brief covering use, references, approval criteria and the person responsible.

agency_d05.subject: “It looks different” needed another sentence
agency_d05.preheader: Turn a vague opinion into useful review feedback.
agency_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Inés received a comment about a chair:

“It looks different.”

She could change things blindly or find out what the client was comparing.

She asked them to identify the detail and reference. The next reply was more useful: “In the approved photo, the arm ends level with the backrest. In this version, it is lower.”

Now there was something specific to check.

You can structure feedback with four fields: observed detail, reference, difference and requested decision.

For example: “Right arm · approved side photo · different height · review before approval.”

If you have an easyrender result, compare it with the reference before deciding what needs correcting or how to proceed. Do not assume every detail can be edited directly in the tool.

If you have not produced it yet, prepare the same form so the first review uses shared criteria.

Inés had feedback she could interpret. The conversation identified what was preventing approval.

Turn one observation or review criterion into a sentence with a detail, reference, difference and decision.
agency_d05.action: Turn one observation or review criterion into a sentence with a detail, reference, difference and decision.

agency_d10.subject: “Which of these files should I use?”
agency_d10.preheader: A delivery note saves the client from reconstructing the project.
agency_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Inés delivered the model and received an unexpected question:

“Which file should I use in the presentation?”

Several versions appeared in the conversation. Delivery needed context.

She prepared this note:

“File: chair-presentation-v2. Intended use: commercial presentation. Checked: opening and appearance in the agreed environment. Pending: final finish approval. This version replaces the earlier one for that review.”

Adapt this format using your actual project details. Name the file, use, checks and outstanding decision. Do not mark a test as completed if it has not happened.

Before delivering an asset produced with easyrender, verify its destination and the access needed by the recipient. A file extension alone does not confirm that all materials and settings will carry over there.

If you do not have a deliverable yet, prepare the note as a template with pending fields.

Inés could continue reviewing the piece. The client now knew which version to comment on.

Write a delivery note naming the file, use, actual checks and outstanding decision.
agency_d10.action: Write a delivery note naming the file, use, actual checks and outstanding decision.

agency_d20.subject: Who had budgeted for the meeting?
agency_d20.preheader: A deliverable costs more than the work inside the files.
agency_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Inés had counted model production and review. Then came other tasks: gathering comments, speaking to the approver and adapting the delivery.

She opened the quote. Those hours were missing.

Inés had subtracted tools and direct work from the project fee. Once she included coordination and adaptation, the expected margin shrank. The calculation was incomplete because tasks were missing, not because the project had changed.

The price had not changed. The amount of work counted had.

To judge what you can repeat, separate preparation, production, review, coordination, adaptation and delivery. Work done with easyrender sits alongside the time spent on the other stages.

If you completed a project, use your observations. If you are preparing one, label your estimates as estimates.

It also helps to know who gathers comments and who approves the work. That organisation is part of the service you are pricing, even when it produces no new file.

Add one previously uncounted coordination or delivery task to a real or example quote.
agency_d20.action: Add one previously uncounted coordination or delivery task to a real or example quote.

agency_d28.subject: What can you offer after the first piece?
agency_d28.preheader: Build the next proposal on something you have checked.
agency_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

The client asked Inés whether she could continue with the catalogue.

Before replying, she reviewed what she knew: one piece had passed the agreed check, review time had been recorded, and other shapes remained untested.

She prepared a proposal with its own scope: “We can evaluate this next group using the approved criteria. We will review pieces with untested details separately.”

You can close your preparation in the same way: what you have confirmed, what remains uncertain and which specific work would make sense to offer next.

If you ran a test, use its results and full cost. If not, the next proposal can be that first limited pilot. Neither requires promising an entire catalogue from the outset.

A useful note is: “We can commit to ___ because we have checked ___. Before expanding to ___, we need to validate ___.”

Inés had a reply that explained both the opportunity and the next step needed to deliver it.

Write a next-step proposal grounded in what is checked, with the main outstanding requirement visible.
agency_d28.action: Write a next-step proposal grounded in what is checked, with the main outstanding requirement visible.

product_views_d00.subject: The photo looked good. The connection was missing.
product_views_d00.preheader: One specific question can decide which view you need.
product_views_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. Let’s start by finding what a view of your product needs to explain.

Illustrative story.

Lucía received several images of a lamp and chose the most attractive ones for a presentation.

“Where does the cable come out?” her colleague asked.

She reopened the folder. Every image showed the same side.

Before producing more, she wrote a small brief:

Question: where does the cable come out?
Required view: the base and connection point.
Reference for checking: a real photograph of that area.

The brief gave the next image a purpose without requiring a whole collection.

Try this with one question about your product. The fastening, base or depth of a pocket might matter. If you need to explain movement, use a suitable demonstration; a still view shows only one position.

Your easyrender test will have a clearer purpose when you know which detail to show and which reference to check it against.

Choose one question and complete: “The next view needs to show ___.”
product_views_d00.action: Choose one question and write what the next view must show.

product_views_d02.subject: Lucía’s test started with one piece
product_views_d02.preheader: Prepare a reference that lets you evaluate the next image.
product_views_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Lucía had several photos ready to test. She chose one with two overlapping objects.

Looking again, she paused. If the hidden part changed in the result, she would have no way to check it against the product.

For the first test, she chose a familiar piece and a photo in which she could recognise it clearly. She noted three features before starting:

Object: a table lamp.
Input photo: the piece visible, with no other lamp in front.
Features to review: shade shape, connection to the support and base.

She kept a photograph of the cable connection for later review. Having it as a review reference does not mean the system processes it as another input.

Prepare an equally small easyrender test. Choosing a photo and criteria does not start generation. Before a paid operation, check its cost and confirm it.

Set aside one photo and note the three features you will use to evaluate the result.
product_views_d02.action: Prepare one photo of a piece and three features to review.

product_views_d05.subject: The fastening changed between two images
product_views_d05.preheader: A simple comparison before approving your views.
product_views_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Lucía switched from the first view to the second. The bag looked the same until she noticed the fastening.

In one image, it was round. In the other, elongated.

Each image looked convincing alone. Together, they described different products.

She placed the views beside a real photograph and wrote:

Feature: fastening shape.
Reference: round fastening in the product photograph.
Result: matches in the first view; difference pending review in the second.

Use this format for the silhouette, parts and details that identify your object. Comparing generated images can reveal contradictions. The real reference helps establish which matches the product.

If you have easyrender views, review them before use. If you are still preparing a test, mark the features in your photo that you will compare when the result arrives.

You do not need to judge everything from memory or approve a set because one image is attractive.

Choose one feature and note what matches, what differs or what you cannot check yet.
product_views_d05.action: Review one feature against its reference, or prepare that criterion if you do not yet have views.

product_views_d10.subject: The information was there. Nobody could find it.
product_views_d10.preheader: Check whether someone can locate the detail they need.
product_views_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Lucía had included the lamp’s connection in the gallery. Her colleague opened the presentation on a phone and asked where it was again.

The image existed. Several similar views came before it.

To check the order, she gave him a task:

“Show me where the cable comes out, using only this presentation.”

She waited without pointing to the answer. She noted where he stopped and where he looked next. That observation suggested what to move or clarify.

Try this with a product page, document or image set you already have. You do not need newly generated content.

Choose a question the presentation should answer and let someone find it: locate a fastening, distinguish two finishes or identify what is included.

This can reveal a comprehension problem. It does not prove a sales improvement, but it can suggest a specific correction before you produce more content.

Ask someone to answer one question using your presentation and record where they struggle.
product_views_d10.action: Run a one-question comprehension check with one person.

product_views_d20.subject: The images were ready. Delivery was still waiting.
product_views_d20.preheader: Find the stage holding up publication.
product_views_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Lucía finished the images and told her team. The following day, they were still missing from the presentation.

Someone needed to select the approved ones, adapt their sizes and confirm who would deliver them.

She reconstructed one piece with this example record:

Production: finished.
Review: two images still need checking.
Adaptation: waiting for final selection.
Delivery: owner not yet confirmed.

Resolving approval was the next improvement. Faster generation would not remove that wait.

If you have prepared an asset, trace its steps from the reference to actual use. If not, use an earlier image delivery to find where your work tends to stall.

Generation time is one part of the process. Its usefulness to you also depends on the work required to reach an accepted image that is used.

You can use easyrender for production and keep this record to evaluate the complete path.

Identify one outstanding step, who can resolve it and what they need to do so.
product_views_d20.action: Identify one outstanding step, its owner and the information needed to resolve it.

product_views_d28.subject: Lucía chose what the next image needed to do
product_views_d28.preheader: Close the test with a decision you can explain.
product_views_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Lucía opened the folder to prepare more views. First, she read a note from the previous presentation:

“The connection is easy to find. The size is still unclear.”

She could request another angle, but this question needed a scale reference and verified measurements. She changed the next resource she planned to prepare.

Her decision read:

Clear already: where the connection is.
Still unclear: how much space the lamp occupies.
Next resource: size information from a checked source.

Close your own test with these three lines. If you have not produced a result, use the question you identified and note what information you still need to decide how to show it.

The next step might be another view, exploring the shape in 3D or improving an existing resource. Choose based on what the viewer still needs to understand.

This welcome series ends here. You do not need a complete collection to reach a useful decision.

Write what you will repeat, change or postpone, and the specific reason for that choice.
product_views_d28.action: Choose whether to repeat, change or postpone a resource and justify it with a specific need.

method_fit_d00.subject: Two people were looking at the same model
method_fit_d00.preheader: One wanted to show it. The other needed a measurement.
method_fit_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. Let’s start by clarifying what you need from a 3D representation.

Illustrative story.

Andrés showed a model on screen. His colleague rotated it and recognised the object she needed for a proposal.

Someone else asked:

“Can we get the measurement of this joint from it?”

They were looking at the same file with two different briefs.

Andrés wrote two examples:

Presentation: show the shape and check that the object is recognisable.
Assembly: verify dimensions and fit using suitable sources and tests.

For the first use, a visual representation can be a useful starting point. For the second, a model generated from a photo does not itself establish the required measurements.

This distinction helps you choose what to test and how to evaluate it. It also applies if you arrived looking for photogrammetry: your intended result should guide the method.

With easyrender, you can evaluate a visual test against references of the object. Before starting, identify the decision it needs to support.

Complete one sentence: “I need the model so someone can ___.”
method_fit_d00.action: Define the model’s use and the decision it needs to support in one sentence.

method_fit_d02.subject: One photo to start, another to check
method_fit_d02.preheader: Prepare a test you can evaluate against real references.
method_fit_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Andrés had a chair photograph and wanted to show its shape in a proposal. The image showed the front clearly but hid the back.

He could begin a visual test. To approve it, he would also need to check what the photo did not show.

He prepared this sheet:

Use: present the chair’s shape.
Input: available front photograph.
Criteria: silhouette, legs and backrest structure.
Missing reference: rear photograph to check the hidden area.

The sheet separated what he could evaluate immediately from what needed to remain pending.

Prepare an easyrender test the same way. Additional references support your review here; they do not imply the system processes all of them as inputs.

Choose a familiar object and a specific visual use. If the brief requires measurements or fit, include the technical source and validation that requirement needs.

Preparing the test does not execute a paid operation. Before generating, check the current cost and decide how much to spend evaluating it.

Prepare one piece’s sheet: use, available photo, acceptance criterion and missing reference.
method_fit_d02.action: Prepare a four-field test sheet for one piece.

method_fit_d05.subject: The model opened. Andrés still had to approve it.
method_fit_d05.preheader: Make the acceptance test as specific as the brief.
method_fit_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Andrés opened the file and turned it on screen.

“It works.”

His colleague pointed to the backrest. Its shape needed another check before joining the proposal.

Opening the file had answered a technical question. They still needed to decide whether it suited the brief.

Andrés wrote this acceptance example:

Requirement: recognise the backrest structure.
Test: compare that view with a real photograph.
Evidence: recorded matches and differences.
Decision: usable for the proposal or pending review.

Adapt this to your chosen use. A presentation needs the relevant details to be visible; another environment may add compatibility, performance or verified measurement requirements.

If you have a result, compare it against one specific condition. If you are still preparing the test, write how you will check that condition when the file arrives.

A small decision like this helps prevent approving something on general impression that another person must later reassess.

Choose one requirement, write its acceptance test and define what would be sufficient.
method_fit_d05.action: Define and, if a result exists, apply an acceptance test for one requirement.

method_fit_d10.subject: Andrés added one sentence to the delivery
method_fit_d10.preheader: Explain what the model has been checked for and what is still pending.
method_fit_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Andrés sent a model for a presentation. Later, the file reached someone who wanted to use it to prepare an assembly.

The conversation returned to what had been reviewed and what could be treated as verified.

For the next delivery, he added this note:

“Representation prepared for the visual proposal. The silhouette has been compared with the stated references. Dimensions and component fit have not been validated for manufacturing.”

The note travelled with the file and preserved the scope of its review.

Adapt it to your project without claiming checks you have not performed:

“Prepared for ___. Reviewed using ___. Still pending ___.”

If no result exists, use future wording: “Will be prepared for…; will be reviewed using…”. This helps agree the recipient’s expectations before production.

An asset can pass between people with different needs. Stating its intended use and limits lets the next team decide which additional checks it requires.

Write those three lines for the next person who will use your model.
method_fit_d10.action: Write a delivery note stating use, checks and pending work without implying unperformed verification.

method_fit_d20.subject: The cheaper quote left one task out
method_fit_d20.preheader: Compare the work you need completed as well as the price.
method_fit_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Andrés had two proposals for the same project. One looked cheaper, but its scope left adaptation to the final destination to his team.

Before choosing, he compared one specific line:

Required delivery: asset reviewed in the destination application.
Proposal A: file and review in that environment included.
Proposal B: file included; adaptation and review still pending.

They were not yet prices for the same completed work.

Compare quotes or methods this way. Include only tasks your use requires: preparation, production, review, adaptation and delivery, as applicable.

If an option offers capabilities you do not need, you do not have to pay for them to consider your brief complete.

When evaluating easyrender, combine the current quote with the work you will need to perform afterwards. Generation cost is one part of obtaining a useful deliverable.

Choose one necessary task and check whether it is included, who will do it and how it will be validated.
method_fit_d20.action: Compare one necessary task across options and clarify its owner and validation.

method_fit_d28.subject: Andrés could explain what it was useful for
method_fit_d28.preheader: End the month with a specific decision about your project.
method_fit_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Andrés reviewed his test. The representation helped explain the shape in a proposal, but it still did not establish the measurements needed for another brief.

He saved a decision for each use:

Visual proposal: continue with the agreed references and review.
Assembly check: use a process that can validate the required measurements.

The same result had helped him separate two paths.

Close your evaluation with a short note:

“For ___, my evidence is ___. My next decision is ___ because ___.”

If you have not tested yet, write the condition missing from that decision. It might be an object reference, a recipient’s requirement or a maximum budget. You do not need to describe a result that does not exist.

You might continue with easyrender for that visual use, adjust the test or choose another approach. What matters is explaining what fits and what still needs checking.

This closes your welcome series.

Record one decision and the evidence, or missing information, that supports it.
method_fit_d28.action: Document a decision to continue, adjust or choose another approach, with its supporting reason.

general_d00.subject: Pablo needed to explain one thing
general_d00.preheader: Your intended use helps you choose the first test.
general_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. These emails will help you prepare a small test and decide whether the result is useful to you.

Illustrative story.

Pablo wanted to explain an object’s shape to someone. He sent a photograph and received a question:

“Does that opening go all the way through?”

The image did not make it clear.

Before producing more content, he wrote his goal: “I want someone to understand this opening.”

He could find a view that showed it, explore the shape through a 3D representation or provide another reference. First, he needed to specify what he wanted to explain.

This works for a presentation, catalogue, commission or personal test. It does not depend on a particular profession.

“I need to compare two objects’ shapes” is a visual goal. “I need their exact measurements” requires reliable information that a generated image does not establish on its own.

With easyrender, a specific question can guide both production and review.

Complete this sentence for your case: “I want to use the result to understand or show ___.”
general_d00.action: Define what you want the result to help someone understand or see.

general_d02.subject: The first test fitted into one photo
general_d02.preheader: Prepare a familiar object and a question you can check.
general_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Pablo was about to start with a box full of pieces. He chose one first: an object he knew and could inspect from every side.

That would make it easier to compare the representation with something real.

He prepared this test:

Object: a small plant pot.
Input reference: a photo showing the piece clearly.
Goal: show its silhouette and the shape of its rim.
Check: compare those two features with the object.

He did not need to solve every possible use of 3D in his first attempt.

Prepare your test using the same format. If you already have a project, use its current reference. You do not need another project for this exercise.

When starting from an image, keep the object or additional references to check areas it does not show. Before a paid operation in easyrender, review the quote and decide whether it fits your budget.

Preparing the photo does not execute generation.

Choose one piece and note its reference photo and two features you want to check.
general_d02.action: Prepare one piece, a reference photo and two features to check.

general_d05.subject: “It looks good” was not enough for Pablo’s review
general_d05.preheader: A specific comparison makes the decision easier.
general_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Pablo turned his object’s representation. His overall impression was good, but he was unsure how to answer “Is it ready?”

He returned to his two chosen features: silhouette and rim.

His review read:

Silhouette: matches the reference in the checked views.
Rim: an area hidden in the photo still needs review.
Decision: keep this version, pending that check before use.

Make the same specific review with an easyrender result or another visual resource you are preparing.

Choose a feature that matters for your use and compare it with a reliable reference. Describe any difference or missing information. “The rim is different” supports a clearer decision than an overall impression of appearance.

If you do not have a result, write the criterion you will apply to that feature when it arrives. Preparing the review does not require starting another operation.

Record one decision for that feature: matches, needs review or not enough information to check.
general_d05.action: Give one feature a decision: matches, needs review or missing information.

general_d10.subject: “Where do I open it?” came after delivery
general_d10.preheader: A short note gives the file a clear intended use.
general_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Pablo sent the file and considered the task finished.

The reply came straight back:

“Where do I open it, and what should I check?”

The result was prepared, but the next step needed explaining.

He added this note:

“This asset is for reviewing the shape in the agreed presentation. It has been tested in the stated environment. The highlighted detail still needs confirmation before approval.”

Adapt the note using three fields: intended use, completed check and outstanding decision. Include only verified facts. If the file has not been tested at its destination, mark that as pending.

The same note helps if the next user is you a few days later. It reminds you why you prepared the asset and what remains to do.

If you do not have a result yet, write the brief in the future tense. Thinking about delivery helps you check requirements before production.

Complete a three-line note for your asset’s next use.
general_d10.action: Write a note covering intended use, completed check and outstanding decision.

general_d20.subject: The second piece only looked similar at first
general_d20.preheader: Change one thing to understand what you can repeat.
general_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Pablo’s first test had helped explain a simple object. Next, he chose a similar shape with a more complex detail.

Before starting, he noted what he wanted to learn:

Keep: presentation use and review criterion.
Change: this piece has an opening the first did not.
Check: whether that opening is represented usefully and can be verified.

The comparison would help him identify which parts of the process still worked and which required another reference or review.

Prepare the same plan for a next piece. If you have not tested the first, keep this plan pending. You do not need to run two tests at once to complete the exercise.

One useful result does not establish that every material or geometry will behave the same way. Choosing a specific difference helps you learn without turning the next test into an open-ended project.

Before a paid operation, review its current cost too.

Write what you would keep and the one relevant difference you would evaluate in the next piece.
general_d20.action: Plan a next piece with one retained criterion and one relevant difference.

general_d28.subject: Pablo wrote down why he would use it again
general_d28.preheader: Continuing, adjusting and waiting can each be useful decisions.
general_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Pablo saved the result with his notes. He had explained the shape he wanted to show, and he had also spent time gathering references and reviewing the file.

To decide whether to repeat the process, he wrote:

“It suits this presentation because it clarifies the detail I wanted to show. I would repeat it for a similar object when I have enough references to review it.”

His decision connected usefulness with the work required.

Close your test with a similar sentence. Include what you needed, what evidence you have and what you would do next. When considering cost, count preparation and review alongside generation.

If you have not tested yet, identify what prevents a decision: a missing reference, an unclear use or uncertainty about the result. Writing that down is more useful than treating an unfinished project as completed.

This email closes your easyrender welcome series.

Choose continue, adjust or postpone, and write one reason you can check in your own case.
general_d28.action: Choose continue, adjust or postpone and document a verifiable reason.

api_d00.subject: The API responded. The model still needed delivering.
api_d00.preheader: Start with one task you can verify from beginning to end.
api_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. These emails will help you prepare an integration that ends with a usable model.

Illustrative story.

Diego showed the API response.

“It works.”

His colleague opened the product page.

“Where can I see it?”

A job had been created, but the result, review and delivery to the right destination were still missing.

Diego wrote a small test: “Start with this chair photo and reach a file we can review for its product page.”

Underneath, he listed five checks:

Product identified → job recorded → result available → piece reviewed → destination tested.

Each answered a different question. Which product was it? Which job should they check? Did a file exist? Did it represent the chair? Would it work in that application?

You can use this path to prepare your easyrender integration. You do not need to process a catalogue yet. Define one deliverable you would know how to accept.

Diego’s next demo would start where his colleague expected to find the result.

Write one sentence for your test: “Start with ___ and deliver ___ so that ___ can use it in ___.”
api_d00.action: Write down the deliverable your first test must complete.

api_d02.subject: Diego left ninety-nine products waiting
api_d02.preheader: The first test needed one well-chosen piece.
api_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Diego had prepared a list of one hundred products to test the integration.

His colleague pointed to one:

“We know this one well. If a part changes, we will notice.”

They chose that chair and saved an input photo alongside references for reviewing the result. The rest of the catalogue could wait.

Their test sheet read:

Object: chair from the catalogue.
Use: visual review for a product page.
Features to check: four legs, backrest shape and seat joint.
Destination: the team’s chosen application.
Limit: one test, with the cost reviewed before approval.

This example does not verify measurements or mechanical fit. It defines a visual review someone can perform using references of the actual product.

For your first test, choose a familiar piece and three features that matter for its use. If the photo hides one, keep another reference for review. That does not mean the API processes every image as an input.

Diego now had a test he could explain without showing code.

Complete the sheet for one product before starting a paid operation.
api_d02.action: Prepare a test sheet for one familiar product.

api_d05.subject: The “Retry” button appeared too soon
api_d05.preheader: Three messages that distinguish waiting from a confirmed result.
api_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Diego’s screen stopped waiting and displayed “Retry”.

“Has the generation failed?” his colleague asked.

He did not know yet. His application’s timeout did not confirm the remote job’s state.

Before changing the button, he wrote three messages:

Job confirmed in progress: “Your model is still processing. You can check this job.”

State still unknown: “We are checking the result. We have kept the job reference.”

Job finished and file available: “The model is ready for review.”

These are interface examples, not official API state names. They must match what the service has confirmed.

Diego saved the job identifier with the original product. He could now check the same job before offering another generation.

If your application did not receive an identifier, consult the documented strategy for that situation. Do not assume repeating the request is harmless or that a particular duplicate-protection mechanism exists.

The next wait in Diego’s demo had a message and an understandable action.

Check what your integration does when a wait expires: does it query the existing job or start another?
api_d05.action: Check what the integration does when a wait expires.

api_d10.subject: The file opened. The joint did not match.
api_d10.preheader: Separate technical checks from visual approval.
api_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Diego’s integration had found the file. The viewer opened it and the job record was complete.

His colleague brought up the reference photo.

“This joint does not match.”

Diego had built a useful technical check. Deciding to use this version required more.

They split the review into three lines:

Technical: the file exists and opens in the intended environment.
Visual: it preserves the required product features, compared with reliable references.
Use: a responsible person approves this version for the agreed destination.

An example result would be: “Technical check passed; difference at the seat joint; visual approval pending.”

This record makes it possible to act on a specific difference without treating completed generation as automatic approval. It does not assume the detail can be edited inside easyrender.

You can make the comparison manually. An assistant describing a file does not replace a reliable review of the piece.

Diego kept the technical check and added the decision that had been missing.

For an available result, record what has been checked and what remains pending under those three headings.
api_d10.action: Record the technical, visual and intended-use review of an available result.

api_d20.subject: Diego changed the number he was dividing by
api_d20.preheader: An example of calculating the cost of a usable asset.
api_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Diego was comparing processes by their cost per request.

His colleague asked another question:

“What does it cost us to get a piece we can actually use?”

They opened the pilot sheet and separated generation, review, preparation and accepted assets.

Cost per accepted asset = total process costs / number of accepted assets.

Each team needs to fill in that calculation with its actual costs and reviewed pieces it can use.

Counting only requests would have excluded much of the work. A complete comparison also needs relevant storage, operations and adaptation costs, with refunds accounted for once.

This calculation does not require the whole process to be automated. It helps reveal where human work is concentrated and which change is worth trying next.

If you do not yet have accepted assets, the unit cost remains unknown. Dividing by attempts does not replace it.

Diego could now compare processes using a unit his colleague recognised.

If you have a reviewed sample, calculate its cost per accepted asset. If not, prepare the sheet with generation, review and accepted assets, leaving missing figures blank.
api_d20.action: If you have a reviewed sample, calculate its cost per accepted asset. If not, prepare the sheet with generation, review and accepted assets, leaving missing figures blank.

api_d28.subject: The demo was finished. The next decision was not.
api_d28.preheader: A useful conclusion whether you tested or are still preparing.
api_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Diego could show a product that had passed through the full integration.

Before adding the rest of the catalogue, his colleague asked what still required work.

They wrote a short note:

Worked: the file reached the intended destination.
Took more work: reviewing certain details.
Still pending: checking another product family.
Decision: improve the review before expanding.

The note separated observations from expectations.

If you have tested your integration, use these four lines with your own results. Include failed jobs and review time. A sample containing only easy successes can hide the actual effort.

If you have not tested yet, your decision can still be specific: “I need to confirm the destination”, “I need more references” or “This project will wait”. You do not need to generate a model to identify a blocker.

Expanding, adjusting and postponing are different decisions. Choose the one supported by what you know today.

Write down that decision and the information that would make you reconsider it. That becomes a starting point for your next project.
api_d28.action: Write down your integration decision and the information that could change it.

mcp_d00.subject: The assistant needed a smaller brief
mcp_d00.preheader: Start with one task you can review in a single pass.
mcp_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. We will help you prepare 3D tasks you can give your assistant and review against clear criteria.

Illustrative story.

Nora typed:

“Turn my catalogue into 3D.”

Then she looked at her folder: duplicate photos, similar products and several versions with the same name.

She replaced the request with one piece:

“I want a visual representation of this chair for its product page. This is the input photo. Before starting a paid operation, explain the current cost and wait for my confirmation. When finished, identify the result and what needs reviewing.”

The brief now had an input, a use and an approval point. Nora also knew what completion meant: an identified result she could compare with the real chair.

With easyrender connected through MCP, that task can form part of the conversation. The effective scope depends on the client and available permissions. A written instruction does not create a technical spending limit.

Nora had defined one task she could accept or review.

Write your brief in one sentence: “Using this reference, I want to prepare ___ for use in ___.”
mcp_d00.action: Define one limited visual task for the assistant.

mcp_d02.subject: Nora had three photos of the same chair
mcp_d02.preheader: Choosing the reference removes an ambiguous decision.
mcp_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Nora’s folder contained three photos of a chair. One showed another finish and another belonged to an older version.

Before requesting the model, she prepared a note:

Product: chair from the current collection.
Chosen input: photo of the finish we will present.
Review references: back and seat joint.
Important features: four legs, backrest curve and support positions.

The additional images were references for checking the result. The note did not claim the workflow would process them all as inputs.

You can adapt this brief using your own files. If names are ambiguous, identify the exact image so both you and the assistant know which one was selected.

Also check that you can use the material for this project. Keep keys and credentials out of the reference files.

Nora no longer depended on a request such as “use the good one”. The input and review were separate before she approved generation.

Prepare this note for one piece and mark three features you will check when a result exists.
mcp_d02.action: Identify an unambiguous reference and three features to review.

mcp_d05.subject: The chair looked good. Nora brought up the photo.
mcp_d05.preheader: Three comparisons before approving a result.
mcp_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Nora turned the chair model. She liked its appearance.

Then she opened the reference beside it. The backrest curve did not match.

Instead of writing “it looks wrong”, she recorded a specific observation:

Feature: backrest curve.
Reference: side photograph.
Difference: the result gives it a different shape.
Decision: review required before using this version.

Repeat this record for three features that identify your product: legs, fastenings, joints or important openings.

Compare the result manually with reliable references. If your assistant supports image analysis, it may help organise observations, but do not treat its assessment as verified or ask it to check an unseen area.

Record what you cannot verify yet too. This helps identify missing information without confusing a convincing image with an accurate representation.

Nora could now explain what prevented approval. The observation did not guarantee that this detail could be edited inside easyrender.

Compare three features of an available result and record one decision: acceptable for this use, needs review or missing a reference.
mcp_d05.action: Compare three result features and record a review decision.

mcp_d10.subject: Nora returned to the chat with seven saved lines
mcp_d10.preheader: A simple receipt for continuing an existing task.
mcp_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Nora opened a long conversation from the previous day. She remembered the product but was unsure of the job’s state and what she had approved.

For the next session, she saved this receipt:

Product: [your reference].
Job: [identifier].
Last checked state: [state and time].
Available result: [reference, if any].
Approved operations: [scope and limit].
Confirmed spending: [amount and unit, or pending].
Next step: [check status or review].

Prepare it manually or ask the assistant to fill it in using verified information. Do not include credentials.

When you return, try: “Check the job in this receipt and tell me its current state. If another paid operation is needed, wait for my approval.”

The receipt preserves context; current information must still be checked with the service. It also does not replace the connected client’s permission controls.

Nora had a specific reference to continue from, even though the previous conversation remained long.

Save this receipt for an identified task. Mark unconfirmed details as pending instead of filling them in from memory.
mcp_d10.action: Save a verified receipt for an existing task.

mcp_d20.subject: The second piece did not need a new conversation
mcp_d20.preheader: What to keep from a brief and what to check again.
mcp_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Nora’s first piece had passed review. For the next, she began copying the entire conversation.

Then she noticed a difference: the new product had another type of joint.

She separated reusable instructions from details that needed changing:

Keep: intended use, job identification method and approval point.
Update: product, input photo, review features and current cost.
Check again: the new result and its references.

The template saved writing without treating two products as equivalent.

You can save a brief like this: “Keep the agreed use and procedure. For this piece, replace the input with [reference] and review [features]. Present the plan and cost before starting paid work.”

Approval for one piece does not automatically extend to another. You also do not need a batch-processing feature to prepare a reusable brief.

Nora could repeat what had worked while paying attention to what changed.

Adapt a brief for a next piece and leave it prepared without starting generation. If the first result has not been reviewed, make that review a condition before repeating it.
mcp_d20.action: Adapt a brief for a next piece and leave it prepared without starting generation. If the first result has not been reviewed, make that review a condition before repeating it.

mcp_d28.subject: Nora looked at the work she was still doing
mcp_d28.preheader: Decide which tasks are worth continuing to delegate.
mcp_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Nora remembered the assistant completing part of a task quickly. Reviewing the project, she also found time spent preparing references and checking the result.

She wrote four lines:

Prepared: identified the correct photo.
Delegated: the agreed task with the assistant.
Reviewed: the piece’s features and destination.
Would repeat: the brief, keeping that review.

The list separated a convenient conversation from completed work.

If you have used the workflow, add the human time and costs you can confirm. Compare similar tasks before estimating savings. One simple piece may not represent the whole catalogue.

If you have not tested yet, close the month by identifying what is missing: connecting a compatible client, choosing a reference or deciding how you would use the result. Recognising that condition does not require starting generation.

Nora ended with a decision about her next task rather than a count of messages sent to the assistant.

Write down which task you would repeat, adjust or postpone, and what you need to check before taking the next step.
mcp_d28.action: Record a task to delegate, adjust or postpone and its next condition.

formats_d00.subject: Valeria had a GLB. Where would she use it?
formats_d00.preheader: Start with the destination of your first delivery.
formats_d00.body:
Welcome to easyrender. We will help you prepare a model for a specific use, from reviewing the file to handing it over.

Illustrative story.

Valeria had a GLB and two requests: show it in a presentation and use it on a product page.

Before sending the same file to both teams, she asked where they would open it.

The replies named different applications and requirements that remained untested.

She prepared a sheet for the first destination:

Use: show the product in a presentation.
Environment: application and version selected by the recipient.
Preserve: relevant shape and materials.
Acceptance: open the piece and perform the intended presentation.

The format’s name started the conversation. A test at the destination would establish whether that asset worked there.

If you start with an easyrender GLB, check the receiving environment’s requirements before promising compatibility. Another format may require conversion and a fresh review.

Valeria chose one destination for her first delivery. Other applications would need their own checks.

Complete the sheet with one use and the tool in which you need to open your model.
formats_d00.action: Choose a destination and define its acceptance test.

formats_d02.subject: Valeria tested one piece before preparing the rest
formats_d02.preheader: A small test can clarify the whole delivery.
formats_d02.body:
Illustrative story.

Valeria’s team had chosen where to open the model. Several pieces still needed preparing.

Before continuing, they tested an existing file in that application.

They left a short note:

Opening: the file opens.
Appearance: required materials look as expected.
Use: the recipient can perform the intended presentation.
Pending: one check still unconfirmed.

Use these four lines for your first test. Record the file and version so the result belongs to an identifiable piece.

If real-world scale matters, add a comparison with reliable measurements. Appearance on screen does not verify that information.

If the file will not open or its appearance changes, record exactly what you observe and keep the original. The test should produce a specific question before you repeat the process across every product.

Valeria left the other pieces waiting until she knew what each delivery would need.

Use a file you already have to test the chosen destination and complete the four lines. You do not need to generate another piece to check this path.
formats_d02.action: Test an available file in its destination and record the result.

formats_d05.subject: The material changed when the file opened
formats_d05.preheader: Describe the problem before rebuilding a model blindly.
formats_d05.body:
Illustrative story.

Valeria opened a piece in the destination application. One area looked different from the reference.

Her first thought was to request another model. Before doing that, she kept the original file and described the change:

File and version: the piece being tested.
Destination: application and version.
Expected: the appearance in the approved reference.
Observed: the affected area and how it appears.
Scope: whether it also happens in another available check.

The note did not identify the cause yet. It clarified what changed and where the problem appeared.

You can add an authorised screenshot without unnecessary private information. Keep relevant error messages too, with credentials removed.

The next adjustment should follow the diagnosis: file, import or destination requirements. A conversion completing without an error does not prove the issue is fixed.

Valeria had an explanation someone could investigate. She had not yet spent effort replacing an asset without knowing whether it caused the problem.

If you find a difference, document it using those five fields before changing the file. If you have not tested yet, save the fields as a record for your first import.
formats_d05.action: If you find a difference, document it using those five fields before changing the file. If you have not tested yet, save the fields as a record for your first import.

formats_d10.subject: “Which version should I use for the presentation?”
formats_d10.preheader: The delivery note that accompanies the file.
formats_d10.body:
Illustrative story.

Valeria had a reviewed version. When she sent it to the team, a question arrived:

“Is this the one we tested for the presentation?”

The file was identified, but the checks needed explaining.

She prepared this note:

“This is version [identifier] of product [reference]. We tested it in [application and version] for [use]. We confirmed [observed result]. Still pending: [condition, if any]. Before using it elsewhere, check that destination’s requirements.”

Copy this for your next delivery. Fill in only verified facts and make clear who must resolve an outstanding condition.

Provide file access through the channel authorised for the project. You do not need to publish the asset for someone else to understand how to use it.

If scale matters, state how it was validated. If it remains unverified, do not present it as a real product measurement.

The next recipient could distinguish Valeria’s tested version from a pending proposal.

Prepare the note for a specific version. If you have not reviewed the asset yet, leave its checks marked as pending before sharing it.
formats_d10.action: Prepare the note for a specific version. If you have not reviewed the asset yet, leave its checks marked as pending before sharing it.

formats_d20.subject: Three files were called “final”
formats_d20.preheader: A small record can show which version is actually in use.
formats_d20.body:
Illustrative story.

Valeria changed a detail on a piece. Her folder contained three files called “final”.

She knew which one she had just changed. She did not know which version the sales team still used.

She prepared a simple record:

Product: chair from the collection.
Version: v2.
Change: material reviewed.
Tested destination: presentation.
Version in use: awaiting confirmation.
Owner: person maintaining that presentation.

“Awaiting confirmation” mattered. It avoided treating a version as published just because it was saved in the folder.

Identify files by product, version and purpose. Then record separately where they have actually been used. A copy prepared for the web may need different checks from one intended for close inspection.

Before replacing a file, keep a reference to the earlier version and check which applications depend on it.

Valeria could ask about a specific version and update the right destination.

Record one asset using those six fields, marking unconfirmed use as unknown. If you do not have a file yet, prepare the record for its first version.
formats_d20.action: Record one asset using those six fields, marking unconfirmed use as unknown. If you do not have a file yet, prepare the record for its first version.

formats_d28.subject: Valeria counted the destinations actually in use
formats_d28.preheader: Decide on reuse, even if the first test is still pending.
formats_d28.body:
Illustrative story.

Valeria’s model had several possible applications. When she reviewed the work, only some had actually been used.

She divided the sheet into three lines:

Creation: work needed to obtain and review the asset.
Adaptation: additional work for each destination.
Confirmed use: where that version had actually been used.

A possibility on a list was not yet a saving.

If you have used a model, complete these lines from your observations. This helps distinguish a second application that reuses previous work from one that nearly requires starting again.

If you have not tested yet, choose the destination still to be checked and note its main requirement. You do not need to assign value to applications that do not yet exist.

The next decision might be to reuse, adapt or postpone. It depends on the use you need and the work you can justify, not on the number of available formats.

Valeria ended with a priority destination and a clear outstanding check.

Write down what you will do with your next asset and what evidence you need before investing in another destination.
formats_d28.action: Choose whether to reuse, adapt or postpone a destination using a verifiable criterion.

interactive.title: See how a 3D model rotates
interactive.body: Drag the model to rotate it freely and see how that differs from a 360° photo sequence.

scan.title: Test the one-photo route
scan.body: AI infers geometry from one image. For measured reconstruction, compare a multi-photo capture workflow.

LandingIntent.qualityTitle: Check the result, not just the model name
LandingIntent.qualityBody: Compare the source and result. Fine details, transparent surfaces and unseen sides may need correction; generated geometry is not a measured CAD model.
LandingIntent.galleryBody: Open a model to compare it with the source photo. The gallery includes public models and curated examples. Downloads are available on eligible examples and your own models.

usdz.title: See the model in your browser
usdz.body: Rotate this example in a web viewer. The sample download is a GLB. Quick Look on iPhone uses a USDZ file.

LandingIntent.sampleDisclosure: Opens a 3D model in your browser.

meta.title: 3D models and AR for online stores · Easy Render
meta.description: Turn your product photos into 3D models. Add an augmented reality button and QR code to product pages with a finished model. See setup for Shopify, WooCommerce, PrestaShop or another store.

hero.subtitle: Turn catalogue photos into 3D models. Add a “View in your room” button and QR code to products with a finished model. Pick your platform to see the setup.

steps.four: Paste the HTML into your product page

mock.qrCaption: Scan with your phone to see it in your room
mock.qrAlt: QR code that opens this table in AR on a phone
mock.photoAlt: Product photo of an oak side table
mock.live: Try the demo. The button and QR code open a real model.

phone.title: On a phone: one tap
phone.body: The button opens the interactive 3D model. On compatible phones, shoppers can switch to augmented reality without installing an app.

desktop.title: On a computer: a QR code
desktop.body: Shoppers can scan the QR code to open the model on their phone.

quiet.title: No model, no button
quiet.body: Plugins display the button and QR code once a product has a finished model.

photos.a: The store integration uses the main photo for each product. It skips products without a usable photo and shows which products need attention.

cost.a: Credits are spent as each 3D model starts building, never before you click. The button shows the total for the run, and a model that fails is refunded.

theme.a: In Shopify, add or remove the block using the theme editor. With WooCommerce and PrestaShop, the plugin uses the platform’s built-in placement options.

devices.q: Which phones can open the AR view?
devices.a: iPhones and iPads through Quick Look and Android phones that support Scene Viewer. On a device without AR the page shows the 3D model and the QR code instead.

accuracy.q: How close is the model to the real product?
accuracy.a: The model uses one product photo and estimates the sides it cannot see. Check the finished model before showing it to shoppers. Dimensions are approximate.

remove.q: What happens if I uninstall it?
remove.a: The button disappears from your product pages and the store’s product list is forgotten. The models stay in your Easy Render account.

cost.title: What it costs
cost.note: Example at the pay-as-you-go rate, excluding optional edits. Buy credits in advance. The generation button shows the total before you confirm, and failed models are refunded in credits.

FirstModelAdmin.title: First model experiment
FirstModelAdmin.description: A: free angles, paid 3D. B: one free 3D model after account verification. Enrollment starts at the angle preview, before signup.
FirstModelAdmin.rule: The sample is twice the offer cap, assigned 50/50. Pausing honors existing offers. The cap and deadline are fixed once started.
FirstModelAdmin.cost: Up to {amount} USD in estimated provider cost for the free-model group, including previews. Retries and infrastructure are additional.
FirstModelAdmin.error: Could not update the experiment. Check verification email availability and try again.
FirstModelAdmin.caveat: Primary metric: 30-day paying conversion per assigned visitor, including people who never register. Only complete observation windows are compared. This pilot does not establish LTV or statistical significance.
FirstModelAdmin.costCaveat: These totals have unequal follow-up times and are diagnostic only. Render costs are estimates, may omit failed provider work, and exclude fees and infrastructure. Currencies are kept separate; no mixed-currency margin is calculated.
FirstModelAdmin.pricing: The report also splits cohorts by the existing pricing experiment.
